en: It is not permissible for monks or nuns to accept raw *tāla* fruit while it is still unbroken.
It is permissible for monks or nuns to accept raw *tāla* fruit once it has been broken.
It is permissible for monks to accept ripe *tāla* fruit, whether it is broken or unbroken.
It is not permissible for nuns to accept unbroken ripe *tāla* fruit.
It is permissible for nuns to accept broken ripe *tāla* fruit, provided it has been broken according to the rule and not otherwise broken.

In a village, or a city, or a market town, or a hamlet, or a fortified town, or a port, or a mine, or a harbor, or a trading center, or a royal capital, or a hermitage, or a settlement, or a caravan camp, or a cattle station, or a border region, or a frontier outpost—whether it be surrounded by a wall or not—Nirgranthas may stay for one month during the winter and summer seasons.

In a village or even in a capital city that has an enclosure and an outer area, it is permissible for the *nirgranthas* to stay for two months during the winter and summer: one month inside and one month outside. For those staying inside, alms-round is conducted inside; for those staying outside, alms-round is conducted outside. In a village or even in a capital city that has an enclosure but no outer area, it is permissible for the *nirgranthīs* to stay for two months during the winter and summer.

In a village or even in a capital city that has an enclosure and an outer perimeter, it is permissible for the *nirgranthīs* (female mendicants) to stay for two months during the winter and summer, two months inside [the enclosure], and two months outside. For those staying inside, alms-round is conducted inside; for those staying outside, alms-round is conducted outside. However, in a village or even in a capital city that has only one compound, one gate, and one entrance for exiting and entering, it is not permissible for *nirgranthas* (male mendicants) and *nirgranthīs* to stay together.

In a village, or even up to a royal capital, which is enclosed, has gates, and allows for both exit and entry, it is permissible for both the *nirgranthas* (monks) and the *nirgranthīs* (nuns) to dwell together.

However, it is not permissible for the *nirgranthīs* to dwell in a shop-house, at a street corner, on a crossroads, at a junction of three roads, at a junction of four roads, at a place where four roads meet, or in a market stall.
It is, however, permissible for the *nirgranthas* to dwell in a shop-house, or even up to a market stall.

It is not permissible for nuns to dwell in a lodging with unsecured doors; however, it is permissible for them to dwell there provided that one layer is made inside and one layer is made outside, and the floor is covered with a mat.
It is permissible for monks to dwell in a lodging with unsecured doors.
It is permissible for nuns to carry or use an internal oil-container or a jar-measure.
It is not permissible for Nirgranthas to wear or use an inner oil-vessel or a small jar.
It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to wear or use a cloth-mat.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to stand, sit, lie down, sleep, or doze on the bank of water; nor is it permissible to consume food, drink, soft food, or delicacies there; nor to discharge feces, urine, phlegm, or nasal mucus there; nor to perform recitation (*svādhyāya*), nor to practice spiritual vigilance (*dharmajāgaryā*), nor to assume the posture of the *kāyotsarga*.
It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to dwell in a residence that has been prepared with living matter (*sacittakarma*).

It is permissible for both monks (nirgranthas) and nuns (nirgranthīs) to dwell in a residence that has not been constructed by them. It is not permissible for nuns to dwell in a residence without the supervision of a householder;
it is permissible for nuns to dwell in a residence with the supervision of a householder.
It is permissible for *nirgranthas* to dwell in a garment [or lodging] either with the support of a householder (*sāgāriya*) or without such support.

It is not permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to dwell in a residence belonging to a householder. It is permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to dwell in a residence that is free from householders (*appasāgāriya*).

It is not permissible for *nirgranthas* to dwell in a lodging that is shared with women. It is permissible for *nirgranthas* to dwell in a lodging that is shared with men. It is not permissible for *nirgranthīs* to dwell in a lodging that is shared with men.
It is permissible for nuns to dwell in a lodging that is shared with women. It is not permissible for monks to dwell in a lodging that is shared [with other monks].
It is permissible for nuns to dwell in a lodging that is shared [with other nuns].
It is not permissible for naked mendicants (nirgranthas) to go through the middle of a householder’s family for the sake of obtaining clothing.
It is permissible for female mendicants (nirgranthīs) to go through the middle of a householder’s family for the sake of obtaining clothing.

When a monk has committed an offense and, having resolved that offense, has presented the matter for settlement, another person may, at their own will, accept him or not accept him; at their own will, rise up for him or not rise up for him; at their own will, pay him homage or not pay him homage; at their own will, share food with him or not share food with him; at their own will, live together with him or not live together with him; at their own will, become reconciled with him or not become reconciled with him.

He who attains tranquility possesses right practice (*ārāhaṇā*); he who does not attain tranquility lacks right practice. Therefore, one must attain tranquility by oneself. Why is that? O Venerable One, because asceticism has tranquility as its essence. It is not permitted for monks or nuns to wander during the rainy season retreats; it is permitted for monks or nuns to wander during the winter and summer seasons.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to undertake a journey, to undertake a return journey, or to undertake a journey and return journey in a kingdom that is hostile to another kingdom. Indeed, whichever Nirgrantha or Nirgranthī undertakes a journey, a return journey, or a journey and return journey in a kingdom hostile to another kingdom, or approves of one who does so—transgressing in both ways—he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture (*parihārasthāna*) that is non-expiable (*anugghāiya*).

If a Nirgrantha has entered the house of a householder for the purpose of alms-food and someone should offer him a garment, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth, it is permissible for him to accept it with a formal agreement (*sāgārakaḍa*), place it at the feet of his teacher, and after obtaining permission for a second time, use it as a loan.

If someone should invite a Nirgrantha who has gone outside to a place for study or a place for residence with a garment, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth, it is permissible for him to take that which was offered under a formal agreement, place it at the feet of his teacher, and after requesting permission for a second time, to use it as a loan.

If a nun has entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms-gathering and someone should offer her a garment or other such thing, it is permissible for her to accept it as a formal pledge (*sāgārakaḍa*), place it at the foot of a sacred tree (*pavittaṇīpāya*), and then take possession of it once more after [the donor] has relinquished it.

If someone should offer a garment, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a foot-wiping cloth to a nun who has gone outside to a place for study or a place for residence, it is permissible for her to accept it with a formal agreement (*sāgārakaḍa*), deposit it at the feet of her preceptor (*pravartinī*), and after obtaining permission for a second time, use it as an exchange.
It is not permissible for monks or nuns to accept solid food, soft food, chewable food, or non-chewable food at night or at dawn.
Except for a single bedding-mat (śayyā-saṃstāraka) previously inspected,
it is not permitted for monks or nuns to accept a cloth, an alms-bowl, a blanket, or a broom at night or at dawn.
Except for a single piece of green grass, and even that must have been used, washed, dyed, rubbed, polished, or fumigated.

It is not permitted for a Nirgrantha or a Nirgranthī to travel by way of a long journey at night or at twilight. Nor is it permitted to travel by way of a long journey for the sake of attending a communal feast (*saṅkhaḍi*) or with the intention of going to such a feast.

It is not permitted for a single Nirgrantha to go out or enter outside to a study-ground (*viyārabhūmi*) or a dwelling-ground (*vihārabhūmi*) at night or at twilight. It is permitted for him when accompanied by a second or a third person to go out or enter outside to a study-ground or a dwelling-ground at night or at twilight.

It is not permissible for a nun to go out or enter outside to a place for study or a place for residence alone at night or at twilight. It is permissible for her to go out or enter [outside to a place for study] up to a place for residence with a second, a third, or a fourth person at night or at twilight.

It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to travel as far east as Aṅga-Magadha, as far south as Kauśāmbī, as far west as the region of Thūṇā, and as far north as the region of Kuṇālā; within these limits it is permissible, for this much is the field of the Āryas.
It is not permissible for them to go beyond this; further than that, where knowledge, vision, and conduct do not flourish—so I say.

Within the enclosure of a dwelling, it is not permitted for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to stay even for a single night if rice, or paddy, or mung beans, or black gram, or sesame, or horse-gram, or wheat, or barley, or *javajava* (a type of grain) have been harvested, scattered, strewn, or spread about.

But if he should know thus: "They are not scattered, not strewn, not dispersed, not spread about; they are made into heaps, or made into piles, or made into walls, or made into small mounds, or marked, or sealed, or covered," then it is permissible for the monks or the nuns to wear them during the winter and summer seasons.

But if he should know it thus: "It has not been made into heaps, nor made into piles, nor made into walls, nor made into stacks; it is not placed in storehouses, nor in baskets, nor on couches, nor on garlands; it is not plastered, nor smeared, nor marked, nor sealed, nor covered"—then it is permissible for mendicants or mendicantesses to dwell there during the rainy season.

If, inside the boundary of a dwelling, there should be a jar of fermented liquor or a jar of sour gruel placed down, it is not permissible for monks or nuns to stay there even for a single night. Furthermore, while searching the dwelling, if they do not find [the jar], then it is permissible for them to stay for one or two nights; but whoever stays there beyond one or two nights incurs either a *chēya* (cutting) offense or a *parihāra* (expiation) offense.

If within the enclosure of a dwelling there should be placed jars of cold water or jars of hot water, it is not permitted for monks or nuns to stay there even for a single night. Furthermore, while inspecting the dwelling later on, they might find [the water still there]. In such a case, it is permitted for them to stay for one night or two nights; but if anyone stays there for longer than one or two nights, there shall be either a formal confession (*cheda*) or a period of penance (*parihāra*).

If a fire should burn within the enclosure of a dwelling at all hours of the night, it is not permissible for monks or nuns to stay there even for a single day. Furthermore, while searching the dwelling for another reason, if they do not find [the fire], it is permissible for them to stay for one night or two nights. Should anyone stay there beyond one or two nights, that constitutes either a breach of the rule or a forfeiture.

If a lamp were to burn inside the enclosure of a dwelling throughout the entire night, it is not permitted for monks or nuns to stay there even for a single day; furthermore, if while inspecting the dwelling they do not find [the lamp extinguished], then it is permitted for them to stay for one night or two nights. If, however, there is someone else there who—up until the point where he might cause damage or evict them—they must leave.

Within the boundary of a dwelling, it is not permissible for a monk or a nun to consume—whether for the time being or as a long-term store—any of the following if they have been spilled, scattered, strewn about, or thrown about: alms-food, boiled rice, milk, curds, ghee, butter, oil, molasses, cakes, sweetmeats, or *sihariṇī*.

But if he should know it thus: "It is not scattered, nor strewn, nor dispersed, nor spread out; it is not made into heaps, nor made into piles, nor made into walls, nor made into small mounds; it is marked, sealed, or covered," then it is permissible for the monks or the nuns to use it as clothing during the winter and summer seasons.

But if he should know it thus: "It is not made into heaps, nor made into piles, nor made into walls, nor made into stacks; it is not placed in storehouses, nor in baskets, nor on couches, nor on garlands, nor in jars, nor in small pots; it is not plastered, nor smeared, nor marked, nor sealed, nor covered"—then it is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to dwell there during the rainy season retreat.
It is not permissible for a *nirgranthī* (female ascetic) to dwell overnight in a house where one has gone, or in an open house, at the foot of a bamboo, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air.
It is permissible for a *nirgrantha* (male ascetic) to dwell overnight in a house where he has come, or in an open house, at the foot of a bamboo, at the foot of a tree, or in the open air.
If there is one host who provides lodging, or two, three, four, or five hosts who provide lodging, he should designate one of those places as permissible for his stay and avoid the rest.
It is not permissible for monks or nuns to accept alms from a lay supporter that have not been brought outside and are unshared.

It is not permissible for monks or nuns to accept alms from a lay supporter that have been brought outside but are shared. It is not permissible for monks or nuns to accept alms from a lay supporter that have been brought outside and are unshared.
It is permissible for monks or nuns to accept alms-food brought out from a layperson's house that has been mixed [with other items].

It is not permissible for monks or nuns to take alms-food brought out from a layperson's house that was not mixed and make it mixed. Should any monk or nun take alms-food brought out from a layperson's house that was not mixed and make it mixed, or should they approve of one who does so, they incur a four-month period of penance (parihāra-sthāna) involving demerit (anugghāiya) for both having committed the transgression.
If food has been brought by a householder and accepted by the householder, then if it is offered from there, it is not permissible for him to accept it.

If food has been brought by a householder but not accepted by the householder, then if it is offered from there, it is permissible for him to accept it. If food has been taken out by a householder but not accepted by another [monk], then if it is offered from there, it is not permissible for him to accept it.
If what has been brought out by a householder has already been accepted [by another], then it is permissible for him to accept it from there.
If the householder’s utensils are undivided, unseparated, not set aside, and not removed, then it is not permissible for him to accept them from there.
If the householder’s utensils are divided, separated, set aside, and removed, then it is permissible for him to accept them from there.

Regarding food offered as an oblation for a layman (*sāgāriya*), designated for a shrine (*ceiya*), or brought as a gift (*pāhuḍiyā*); or regarding a set of utensils belonging to a layman that has been finished with, relinquished, or is a temporary loan (*pāḍihāriya*): if the layman gives it, or the layman’s attendant gives it, then even if it is being given, it is not permissible for him to accept it. Regarding food offered as an oblation for a layman, designated for a shrine, or brought as a gift; or regarding a set of utensils belonging to a layman that has been finished with, relinquished, or is a temporary loan: if neither the layman nor the layman’s attendant gives it, but the layman’s wife (*pūyā*) gives it, then even if it is being given, it is not permissible for him to accept it.

If a meal intended for the honor of a householder (*sāgāriya-pūyā-bhatta*) has been designated for a shrine (*uddēsiya*), dedicated to a shrine (*cētiya*), and is not yet relinquished (*nisaṭṭha*) or returned to its proper place (*apāḍihāriya*), and if the householder gives it or the householder’s dependents give it, then as long as it is being given, it is not permissible for him to accept it. If a meal intended for the honor of a householder has been designated for a shrine, dedicated to a shrine, and the household utensils have been used and relinquished, and it is not yet returned to its proper place; and if neither the householder nor the householder’s dependents give it, but the householder himself gives it as an offering of honor (*pūyā*), then as it is being given, it is permissible for him to accept it.

It is permissible for both the *nirgranthas* and the *nirgranthīs* to wear or use these five types of garments, namely: those made of *jaṅgī* (wool), *bhagī* (linen), *sāṇa* (hempen), *pōtta* (cotton), and the fifth, called *tirīḍapaṭṭa* (bark-fiber).

It is permissible for both the *nirgranthas* and the *nirgranthīs* to wear or use these five types of brooms (*rayaharaṇa*), namely: those made of wool, those made of camel-hair, those made of hempen fibers, those with bound handles, and the fifth, those with handles of *muñja* grass.
Thus I say.

It is not permissible for a Nirgrantha monk to stay, sit, lie down, sleep, or doze in the dwelling of a Nirgrantha nun; nor is it permissible for him to consume food, drink, soft food, or delicacies there; nor to discharge feces, urine, saliva, or nasal mucus there; nor to perform recitation, meditate, perform a *kāyotsarga*, or maintain a standing posture there.

It is not permitted for a nun to stay, or even to remain standing, in the dwelling of a monk. It is not permitted for a nun to possess skins with their hair on. It is permitted for a monk to possess skins with their hair on; however, that [skin] must have been used [by him], and not unused; it must be for temporary use (*pāṭihāriya*), and not for non-temporary use; and it must be for one night only, and not for more than one night.
It is not permissible for monks or nuns to wear or use skins that are entirely black.

It is permissible for monks or nuns to wear or use skins that are not entirely black. It is not permissible for monks or nuns to wear or use garments that are entirely black. It is permissible for monks or nuns to wear or use garments that are not entirely black.
It is not permissible for either monks (*niggantha*) or nuns (*nigganthī*) to wear or use uncut garments. It is permissible for either monks or nuns to wear or use cut garments.
It is not permissible for monks to wear or use a waistband (*uggaha-nantaga*) or a chest-band (*uggaha-paṭṭaga*).
It is permissible for nuns to wear or use a waistband or a chest-band.

If a female ascetic (*nirgranthī*) has entered the household of a layman for the purpose of alms and a need for clothing arises, it is not permissible for her to accept a garment under her own authority. It is permissible for her to accept a garment under the authority of a *pravartinī*. If there is no *pravartinī* present there, then whichever teacher (*ācārya*), preceptor (*upādhyāya*), *pravartinī*, elder (*sthavira*), leader of a group (*gaṇin*), holder of the group (*gaṇadhara*), or supervisor of a group (*gaṇāvacchedaka*) she follows while wandering—having placed him before her—it is permissible for her to accept a garment under his authority.

For a Nirgrantha who is undertaking the wandering life for the first time, it is permissible to go forth into homelessness with a dust-cloth (*rayaharaṇa*), a broom (*gocchaga*), and an alms-bowl (*paḍiggaha*), together with three whole (undyed) garments. However, if he has previously been established [in the household life], it is not permissible for him to go forth with a dust-cloth, a broom, an alms-bowl, and three whole garments; rather, it is permissible for him to go forth having taken whatever garments have already been acquired.

When a female ascetic (nigganthī) first goes forth into homelessness, it is permissible for her to go forth with a broom (rayaharaṇa), a dust-pan (gocchaga), and an alms-bowl (paḍiggaha), and with four whole (kasiṇa) garments. However, if she has previously been established [in another order], it is not permissible for her to go forth with a broom, a dust-pan, and an alms-bowl, and with four whole garments; rather, it is permissible for her to go forth having taken whatever garments have already been accepted as property.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to accept garments that have reached them during the first distribution. It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to accept garments that have reached them during the second distribution.
It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to accept garments according to seniority.
It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to accept bedding and mats according to seniority.
It is permissible for a male mendicant or a female mendicant to perform the ritual salutation (kṛtikarma) according to seniority of initiation.

It is not permissible for a *nirgrantha* or a *nirgranthī* to stand, sit, lie down, sleep, or doze within a private house; nor is it permissible to consume food, drink, soft food, or delicacies there; nor to discharge feces, urine, saliva, or nasal mucus; nor to perform recitation (*svādhyāya*), meditate (*dhyāna*), perform a ritual of renunciation (*kāyotsarga*), or maintain a specific posture (*sthāna*). However, if one should know that [a person] is afflicted by illness, aged, infirm, an ascetic, weak, exhausted, or decrepit, and might faint or fall, then it is permissible for him to stand or [perform all the aforementioned acts], up to and including maintaining a specific posture, within a private house.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to explain, expound, proclaim, or preach [the doctrine] within a house, even to the extent of four or five houses, except by means of a single word, a single explanation, a single verse, or a single stanza; and even that must be done while standing, never while sitting.

It is not permitted for monks or nuns to explain, analyze, proclaim, or teach these five great vows together with their respective reflections within a householder’s home, except by means of a single name, a single explanation, a single verse, or a single stanza—and even then, only while remaining stationary, and certainly not while moving about. It is not permitted for monks or nuns to go forth into homelessness without first returning a borrowed bed or bedding.

It is not permissible for monks or nuns to go forth after having personally prepared a bed or bedding belonging to a householder without making it free from impurities. It is permissible for monks or nuns to go forth after having personally made a bed or bedding—whether it be a loan or belonging to a householder—free from impurities.

In this case, if the bedding or matting belonging to the Niggaṇṭhas or Niggaṇṭhīs—whether it be a loaned item or one belonging to a householder—should be lost, it must be sought after. If, while seeking it, it is found, it must be returned to its original owner. If, while seeking it, it is not found, then it is permissible for him to request permission for a second time and continue using the substitute bedding.

On the very day that the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas abandon their bedding and mats, if other Śramaṇas Nirgranthas should arrive suddenly, the prior authorization for the use of the dwelling remains in effect, even if the use is only for as long as the occasion lasts. Furthermore, if there is any furniture belonging to the residence that is inanimate and fit for use, the prior authorization for its use likewise remains in effect, even if the use is only for as long as the occasion lasts.

If those dwellings are unoccupied, unenclosed, and not claimed by others [nor claimed by gods], then the prior permission for the formal taking of possession (*avagraha*) remains valid even for as long as one may stay.

If those dwellings are occupied, enclosed, and claimed by others, then for the sake of the monk’s state, the formal taking of possession must be requested a second time, even if it is only for as long as one may stay.

If, in the intervals between walls, or between partitions, or between walkways, or between fences, or along paths, or in open spaces, the prior authorization for the formal acquisition remains valid, then one may occupy it even for as long as time permits.

If a Niggaṇṭha or a Niggaṇṭhī sees an army encamped outside a village or even a capital city, it is permissible for them to go on their alms-round that very day and return; however, it is not permissible for them to spend the night right there. Should any Niggaṇṭha or Niggaṇṭhī spend the night right there, or should they approve of one who does so, both of them, having transgressed, incur a four-month penance involving forfeiture (*cāummāsiyaṃ parihāraṭṭhāṇaṃ*) which is non-expiable (*anugghāiyaṃ*).

In a village, or even up to a settlement, it is permissible for monks or nuns to occupy and maintain a space by formally taking possession of an area extending at most one *yojana* in every direction; thus I say. Three [offenses] are declared to be non-expiable (*anugghāiya*): namely, performing manual labor, engaging in sexual intercourse, and eating at night.

Three types of those who have gone beyond (pārañciya) are taught, namely: one who has gone beyond through wickedness, one who has gone beyond through negligence, and one who has gone beyond by acting against one another. Three types of those who are not steadfast (aṇavaṭṭhabba) are taught, namely: one who commits theft against fellow members of the community, one who commits theft against those of other faiths, and one who provides a hand-hold [to assist in such acts].
Three types of persons do not qualify for initiation (pavvāvettae), namely: a eunuch, a hermaphrodite, and a leper.

It is not appropriate for these three to have their heads shaved, to be instructed, to be initiated, to eat together with [the community], or to live in communal residence: namely, the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), the one afflicted by epilepsy (*vāiya*), and the impotent man (*kīva*). It is not appropriate for these three to be ordained: namely, the undisciplined, the one obsessed with sensory diversions (*vigai-paḍibaddha*), and the one who has not mastered the fundamental teachings (*aviōsaviya-pāhuḍa*). It is appropriate for these three to be ordained: namely, the disciplined, the one not obsessed with sensory diversions, and the one who has mastered the fundamental teachings. There are three types of persons described as being ill-disposed: namely, the wicked, the deluded, and the one who is agitated.
Three types of persons are declared to be well-behaved: namely, one who is not angry, one who is not deluded, and one who is not obstinate.

If a father, a brother, or a son should embrace a female mendicant (*nigganthī*) who is ill, and she should consent to it, she incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) that is non-expiable (*anugghāiya*) for the offense of indulging in sexual intercourse. If a mother, a sister, or a daughter should embrace a male mendicant (*niggantha*) who is ill, and he should consent to it, he incurs a four-month period of penance that is non-expiable for the offense of indulging in sexual intercourse.

It is not permissible for a *nirgrantha* or a *nirgranthī*, having accepted food or [other requisites] during the first watch of the day, to let it pass until the last watch. If, however, it should by chance have been allowed to pass that time, they must not consume it themselves nor give it to others; rather, having inspected and wiped a secluded, remote, and very clean spot of bare ground (*thaṇḍila*), they should dispose of it there. By consuming it themselves or giving it to others, they incur a four-month penance involving forfeiture (*parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa*) with suspension (*ugghāiya*).

It is not permissible for a *nirgrantha* or a *nirgranthī* to cause food, drink, soft food, or hard food to be brought from beyond half a *yojana*’s distance. If, however, it has already been brought, they should neither eat it themselves nor give it to others; rather, having inspected and wiped a clean, secluded spot on bare ground, they should discard it there. If one eats it oneself or gives it to others, one incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture (*parihārasthāna*) with suspension (*udghātita*).

If a Nirgrantha, having entered the house of a layman for the sake of alms, should receive any kind of food or drink that is insentient but unfit for consumption, there is someone here who is a junior [monk] to be supervised; it is permissible for him to give it to that person or to cause it to be given to them. If there is no junior person here to be supervised, he himself should not eat it, nor should he give it to others; rather, having inspected and wiped a bare spot in a secluded place free from many living beings, he should discard it there.

That which is prepared for those who abide in what is permissible is permissible for those who abide in what is permissible; it is not permissible for those who abide in what is impermissible. That which is prepared for those who abide in what is impermissible is not permissible for those who abide in what is permissible, but it is permissible for those who abide in what is impermissible. Those who abide in what is permissible are "those who abide in the permissible" (kappaṭṭhiya); those who abide in what is impermissible are "those who abide in the impermissible" (akappaṭṭhiya).

If a monk, having departed from his own group (*gaṇa*), should wish to dwell having entered another group, it is not permissible for him to do so without having asked permission from his teacher (*ācārya*), preceptor (*upādhyāya*), instructor (*pravartin*), elder (*sthavira*), head of the group (*gaṇī*), leader of the group (*gaṇadhara*), or superintendent of the group (*gaṇāvacchedaka*). It is permissible for him to dwell having entered another group only after having asked permission from the teacher or up to the superintendent of the group. If they grant him leave, then it is permissible for him to dwell having entered another group; if they do not grant him leave, then it is not permissible for him to dwell having entered another group.

If a *gaṇāvacchedaka* (group leader) should wish to depart from his own group and, having joined another group, dwell there, it is not permissible for that *gaṇāvacchedaka* to dwell having joined another group without first resigning his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is permissible for a *gaṇāvacchedaka* to dwell having joined another group after having resigned his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is not permissible for him to dwell having joined another group without having asked permission from his *ācārya* or [other superiors] up to the *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is permissible for him to dwell having joined another group after having asked permission from his *ācārya* or [other superiors] up to the *gaṇāvacchedaka*.

If they should grant him permission, then it is permissible for him to go and dwell having joined another group; if they should not grant him permission, then it is not permissible for him to go and dwell having joined another group.

If a teacher or preceptor, having departed from his own group (gaṇa), should wish to enter and dwell in another group, it is not permissible for that teacher or preceptor to enter and dwell in another group without first relinquishing his status as a teacher or preceptor. It is permissible for him to enter and dwell in another group only after he has relinquished his status as a teacher or preceptor.

It is not permissible for him to dwell having joined another *gaṇa* without having asked permission from his *ācārya* or up to the *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is permissible for him to dwell having joined another *gaṇa* after having asked permission from his *ācārya* or up to the *gaṇāvacchedaka*.

If they grant him permission, then it is permissible for him to dwell having joined another *gaṇa*; if they do not grant him permission, then it is not permissible for him to dwell having joined another *gaṇa*.

If a monk, having departed from his own group, should desire to dwell having formally entered another group for the sake of communal enjoyment, it is not permissible for him to do so without having requested permission from his teacher (ācārya) or even from the head of the group (gaṇāvacchedaka). It is permissible for him to dwell having formally entered another group for the sake of communal enjoyment only after having requested permission from his teacher or even from the head of the group.

If he should dismiss them, then it is permissible for him to go and dwell, having entered another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment (*sambhoga*), provided that he may obtain therein a higher Dharma and Discipline; thus it is permissible for him to go and dwell, having entered another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment, provided that he may obtain therein a higher Dharma and Discipline. But if he does not obtain therein a higher Dharma and Discipline, then it is not permissible for him to go and dwell, having entered another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment.

If a *gaṇāvacchedaka* should wish to depart from his own *gaṇa* and, for the sake of communal enjoyment, enter another *gaṇa* to dwell there, it is not permissible for that *gaṇāvacchedaka* to do so without first relinquishing his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is permissible for that *gaṇāvacchedaka* to do so only after having relinquished his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka* and then entering another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment to dwell there.

It is not permissible for him, without having asked permission from his teacher (ācārya) or even a leader of a group (gaṇāvacchedaka), to go and dwell in another group with the intention of communal association (sambhoga). It is permissible for him, having asked permission from his teacher or even a leader of a group, to go and dwell in another group with the intention of communal association.

If they grant him permission, then it is permissible for him to go and dwell in another *gaṇa*, having entered into communal association with them; but if they do not grant him permission, then it is not permissible for him to go and dwell in another *gaṇa*, having entered into communal association with them.

If he should obtain a higher Dharma and Vinaya elsewhere, it is permissible for him to enter another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment and dwell there; if he should not obtain a higher Dharma and Vinaya elsewhere, it is not permissible for him to enter another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment and dwell there.

If a teacher or preceptor, having departed from his own group (gaṇa), should desire to enter another group for the sake of communal living (sambhoga) and dwell there, it is not permissible for that teacher or preceptor to do so without first relinquishing his status as a teacher or preceptor; however, it is permissible for him to relinquish his status as a teacher or preceptor and then enter another group for the sake of communal living and dwell there.

It is not permissible for him, without having asked permission from his teacher (ācārya) or even the leader of the group (gaṇāvacchedaka), to go and dwell in another group with the intention of communal association (sambhoga). It is permissible for him, having asked permission from his teacher or even the leader of the group, to go and dwell in another group with the intention of communal association.

If they should grant it to him, then it is permissible for him to go and dwell in another *gaṇa* with the intent of sharing in its communal life; if they should not grant it to him, then it is not permissible for him to go and dwell in another *gaṇa* with the intent of sharing in its communal life.

Where one may obtain the further Dharma and Vinaya, it is permissible for him to enter another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment and dwell there; where one does not obtain the further Dharma and Vinaya, it is not permissible for him to enter another *gaṇa* for the sake of communal enjoyment and dwell there.

If a monk should wish to designate another teacher or preceptor, it is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having requested permission from his teacher, or [his preceptor, or his *kalyāṇamitra*, or his *gaṇī*, or his *gaṇāvacchedaka*]; it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor only after having requested permission from his teacher, or [his preceptor, or his *kalyāṇamitra*, or his *gaṇī*, or his *gaṇāvacchedaka*].

If they provide him [with the necessary assistance], then it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor; if they do not provide him with it, then it is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor. It is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having explained their reasons; it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor after having explained their reasons.

If a *gaṇāvacchedaka* should wish to designate another as his *ācārya* or *upādhyāya*, it is not permissible for him to designate another *ācārya* or *upādhyāya* without first relinquishing his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka*. It is permissible for him to designate another *ācārya* or *upādhyāya* after he has relinquished his office as *gaṇāvacchedaka*.

It is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having first requested permission from his own teacher or, up to and including, the head of the community (gaṇāvacchedaka). It is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor only after having requested permission from his own teacher or, up to and including, the head of the community.

If they provide him with [the necessary materials], then it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor; if they do not provide them, then it is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor. It is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having informed them of the reason; it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor after having informed them of the reason.

If a teacher-preceptor (ācārya-upādhyāya) should wish to designate another as his teacher-preceptor, it is not permissible for him to designate another teacher-preceptor without having relinquished his own status as a teacher-preceptor; it is permissible for him to designate another teacher-preceptor only after having relinquished his own status as a teacher-preceptor.

It is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having first asked permission from his own teacher or [successive ranks] up to the head of the community (gaṇāvacchedaka). It is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor after having asked permission from his own teacher or [successive ranks] up to the head of the community.

If they grant him leave, then it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor; if they do not grant him leave, then it is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor.

It is not permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor without having informed those [original ones] of the reason; it is permissible for him to designate another teacher or preceptor after having informed those [original ones] of the reason.

If a monk should die by night or at dawn, and some monks who are attendants should wish to dispose of that body in a secluded place that is very convenient, provided there is some inanimate equipment belonging to a householder there that is fit for disposal, it is permissible for him to take that which was made available by the householder, dispose of the body in a secluded and very convenient place, and then leave it right there.

If a monk, having committed an offense (*adhikaraṇa*), does not resolve that offense, it is not permissible for him to go out to or enter a householder’s family for the sake of food or drink; nor is it permissible for him to go out to or enter an external area for study (*viyārabhūmi*) or a monastic dwelling (*vihārabhūmi*); nor is it permissible for him to travel from village to village, or to transfer from one group (*gaṇa*) to another, or to spend the rainy season retreat (*vāsāvāsa*). However, wherever he may see his own teacher (*ācārya*) or preceptor (*upādhyāya*) who is highly learned and well-versed in the scriptures (*bāhyāgama*), it is permissible for him to confess (*āloettae*) to them, to repent (*paḍikkamettae*), to feel remorse (*nindettae*), to censure himself (*garahettae*), to reform (*viuṭṭettae*), to purify himself (*visohettae*), to resolve not to commit the act again (*akaraṇatāe abbhuṭṭhettāe*), and to undertake the appropriate penance (*tavo-kamma*) and atonement (*pāyacchitta*). If he has been sent by those [elders] and has come back, he should be readmitted. If he has been sent by them but has not come back, he should not be readmitted. If he is being sent by them but does not come back, he should be expelled (*nijjūhiyavve*).

For a monk who is undergoing the period of probation (*parihārakappa*), it is permissible for his teacher or preceptor (*ācariya-uvajjhāya*) to have him provided with alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) at a single house on that very day; beyond that, it is not permissible for them to give or cause to be given to him any food (*asana*), drink (*pāna*), soft food (*khāima*), or delicacy (*sāima*). However, it is permissible for them to perform some other service (*veyāvaḍiya*) for him, such as helping him to stand up, sit down, or lie down, or assisting him in the disposal of feces, urine, saliva, or nasal mucus, or in cleansing himself. But if he should know that the paths are cut off, and that he is ill, exhausted, thirsty, emaciated, weak, and weary, and might faint or fall, then it is permissible for them to give or cause to be given to him food, drink, soft food, or delicacies.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to cross, whether by swimming or by boat, these five great ocean-going rivers—counted and enumerated—more than twice or thrice within a month. They are as follows: the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarayū, the Kosiya, and the Mahī.

But if he should know thus: "In Erāvaī Kuṇālā, where it is possible to place one foot in the water and one foot on the land, it is permissible within a month to cross over or swim across two or three times; but where it is not possible in this way, it is not permissible within a month to cross over or swim across two or three times."

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to dwell during the winter or summer months in such a lodging that has grass or heaps of grass, straw or heaps of straw, which is not free from insects, living beings, seeds, green plants, dust, or the webs of ants, nor is it covered by a roof.
However, it is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to dwell during the winter or summer months in such a lodging that has grass or [the rest] up to webs, provided it is covered by a roof.
It is not permissible for monks or nuns to dwell during the rainy season retreat in such a lodging where grass, heaps of grass, or even creepers have been placed beneath the threshold.
It is, however, permissible for monks or nuns to dwell during the rainy season retreat in such a lodging where grass, heaps of grass, or even creepers have been placed above the threshold.
Thus I say.

If a deity, having assumed the form of a woman, should take hold of a *nirgrantha*, and that *nirgrantha* should consent to it, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the practice of sexual intercourse. If a deity, having assumed the form of a man, should take hold of a *nirgranthī*, and that *nirgranthī* should consent to it, she incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the practice of sexual intercourse.

If a goddess, having transformed herself into the form of a woman, should take hold of a *nirgrantha*, and that *nirgrantha* should consent to it, he incurs a four-month period of penance (*parihārasthāna*) involving no reduction of the term for sexual misconduct.

If a goddess, having transformed herself into the form of a man, should take hold of a *nirgranthī*, and that *nirgranthī* should consent to it, she incurs a four-month period of penance involving no reduction for sexual misconduct.

If a monk, having created a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) and not having settled that dispute, should wish to enter another group (*gaṇa*) and dwell there, it is permissible for him to undergo a formal reduction (*cheda*) of five days and nights, and after each such reduction has been completed, he may be readmitted to that same group a second time, or as may be deemed appropriate by that group.

If a monk, having accepted food, drink, solid food, or delicacy while the sun has risen, his intention has not ceased, he is settled [in his place], and he is free from doubt, then eats that food; and if afterwards he should know that the sun has not yet risen or has already set, then by discarding what is in his mouth, what is in his hand, and what is in his alms-bowl, or by purifying them, he does not transgress. However, by eating it himself or giving it to others, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the violation of the rule against eating at night.

If a monk, with the intention of rising [before sunrise] and setting [after sunset], while being in a state of doubt within himself regarding the time, accepts food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacy—and consumes it, and he subsequently realizes that the sun has not yet risen or has already set, then for whatever is in his mouth, whatever is in his hand, and whatever is in his alms-bowl, by discarding it or even giving it away, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the offense of consuming food at night.

If a monk, having resolved upon what has not yet set, being free from doubt and with a mind that has attained certainty, accepts food—whether it be solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies—and consumes it as alms, he should later realize: "The sun has not yet risen, or it has already set. Then, while discarding what is in his mouth, what is in his hand, and what is in his bowl, until he has finished giving it away, he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the offense of consuming food at night.

If a monk, having resolved upon [food] while the sun has not yet risen or has already set, and being in a state of uncertainty and doubt, accepts solid food, drink, soft food, or delicacies, and then eats that food; and if he subsequently realizes that the sun had not yet risen or had already set, then while discarding what is in his mouth, what is in his hand, or what is in his alms-bowl—up to the point of giving it away—he incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the offense of consuming food at night.

In this case, if a Niggantha or a Nigganthī, at night or at twilight, should encounter a cloud of smoke containing living beings and food, and while discerning or clearing it away, they do not overstep [the rule]; yet if, having vomited that up, they swallow it back down, they incur an offense involving a four-month period of penance (parihāra-ṭṭhāṇa) without reduction (anugghāiya), due to the consumption of food at night.

If, when a Nirgrantha has entered a householder’s family for the purpose of alms, living beings, seeds, or dust should fall into his bowl, and he is able to separate or purify them, then having inspected it repeatedly and having purified it repeatedly, he may eat or drink it with restraint. But if he is not able to separate or purify them, he should neither eat it himself nor give it to others; rather, having inspected and wiped a clean spot on a bare patch of ground in a secluded place, he should discard it there.

If, while a Nirgrantha has entered the house of a layman for the purpose of alms, water—whether liquid water, ice-cold water, or water sprayed as mist—should fall into his alms-bowl, that food should be eaten if it is hot; but if that food is cold, he should not eat it himself, nor should he give it to others. Having inspected and wiped a clean, open space on a bare patch of ground, he should discard it there.

If a *nirgranthī*, while voiding excrement or urine at night or at dawn, should be touched by any kind of beast or bird, and she should consent to it, she incurs a monthly *anuddhātiya* offense for practicing manual labor (*hastakarma*).

If a nun, while voiding excrement or urine at night or at twilight, or while cleaning herself, should be entered by any kind of beast or bird into any opening, and that nun consents to it, she incurs a four-month penance involving forfeiture for the practice of sexual intercourse (*methuna-pratisēvana*), which is non-expiable (*anugghāiya*).
It is not permitted for a nun to be alone. It is not permitted for a nun to go out or enter a householder’s family for the sake of food or drink while alone.
It is not permissible for a nun to go out to or enter a wandering area or a dwelling area while alone.
It is not permissible for a nun to travel from village to village while alone. It is not permissible for a nun to spend the rainy season retreat while alone.
It is not permissible for a nun to be naked.
It is not permissible for a nun to go barefoot. It is not permissible for a nun to expose her body.

It is not permissible for a nun to perform the practice of heat-exposure (āyāvaṇā) by standing on one foot with her arms raised high above her head, facing the sun, outside of a village or even a settlement. It is permissible for her to perform the practice of heat-exposure while staying inside the vicinity of her dwelling, leaning against a wall, with both feet placed evenly together and her arms hanging down.
It is not permissible for a nun to remain in a standing posture [without support].

It is not permissible for a nun to remain in the *paḍima* (meditative) posture. It is not permissible for a nun to remain with her limbs extended in the *ṭhāṇukkaḍiya* posture. It is not permissible for a nun to remain in the *nēsajjiyā* (squatting) posture.
It is not permissible for a nun to sit in the hero’s posture (vīrāsana). It is not permissible for a nun to sit on a staff-seat (daṇḍāsana).
It is not permissible for a nun to sit in the crooked posture (lagaṇḍaśāyikā).
It is not permissible for a nun to remain with her head covered. It is not permissible for a nun to remain lying on her back.
It is not permissible for a nun to remain with her body bent like a mango tree.
It is not permitted for a nun to remain with one side [of her body] uncovered. It is not permitted for nuns to wear or use a bandage for contracting [the limbs].
It is permitted for monks to wear or use a bandage for contracting [the limbs].
It is not permissible for a nun to stand, sit, recline, or lie down on a seat that has a cushion.
It is permissible for a monk to stand, sit, recline, or lie down on a seat that has a cushion.
It is not permissible for a nun to stand, sit, recline, or lie down on a bench or a plank that has horns (or protruding supports).
It is permissible for naked mendicants (nirgranthas) to sit or lie down on a vessel that has a handle.
It is not permissible for female mendicants (nirgranthīs) to wear or carry a gourd vessel with a handle.
It is permissible for naked mendicants to wear or carry a gourd vessel with a handle.
It is not permitted for Nirgranthas to carry or use a foot-brush made of grass with a handle. It is permitted for Nirgranthas to carry or use a foot-brush made of grass with a handle.
It is not permitted for Nirgranthīs to carry or use a wooden-handled foot-brush.
It is permissible for the *nirgranthas* to possess or use a wooden-handled broom (*dārudaṇḍaka-pāyapuñchaṇa*).

It is not permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to consume or drink one another’s leavings (*moya*), except in cases of severe or agonizing illnesses. It is not permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to consume food that has been left over, even if it is only the size of a leaf, the size of the earth, or even the size of a drop of water, except in cases of severe or agonizing illnesses.

It is not permissible for monks or nuns to smear or anoint their bodies with any kind of oily unguent that has been prepared, except in cases of severe illness. It is not permissible for monks or nuns to rub or massage their bodies with oil, clarified butter, fresh butter, or fat that has been prepared, except in cases of severe illness.

If a monk standing in the stage of probation (*parihārakappa*) should go outside for the sake of service to the elders, and he should happen to transgress, and the elders should know of it—either by his own report or having heard it from others—then afterwards, the legal procedure known as *ahālahusaga* (the lightest penalty) should be initiated against him.

If a female mendicant (nigganthī) has entered the house of a layperson for the purpose of alms-gathering and has received some coarse food (pulāga-bhatta), she may, if she so desires, conclude her meal for that day with that very portion; it is not permissible for her to enter a second house of a layperson for the purpose of alms-gathering on that same day. However, if she does not desire it, it is permissible for her to enter a second house of a layperson for the purpose of alms-gathering. Thus I say.

It is not permissible for either monks or nuns to utter these six kinds of speech, namely: false speech, contemptuous speech, disparaging speech, harsh speech, worldly speech, or to repeat again what has already been said to cause separation.

Six extensions of the *kalpa* are prescribed, namely: speaking in favor of killing living beings, speaking in favor of false speech, speaking in favor of taking what is not given, speaking in favor of lack of restraint, speaking in favor of being no man [in terms of spiritual capacity], and speaking in favor of being a slave. Having extended these six extensions of the *kalpa*, if one does not properly fulfill them, one may fall into that state.

If a thorn, a stake, a splinter, or a pebble should strike a naked mendicant (niggantha) on his foot, and the naked mendicant is unable to remove it or clear it away, then the naked mendicant woman (nigganthī), while removing it or clearing it away, does not transgress [the rule].

If living beings, seeds, or dust should enter into the eye of a naked mendicant, and the naked mendicant is unable to remove it or clear it away, then the naked mendicant woman, while removing it or clearing it away, does not transgress [the rule].
If a thorn, a splinter, gravel, or a pebble should fall into a nun’s foot, and she is unable to remove it or clean it out, then the monk who removes it or cleans it out does not transgress.
If a living being, a seed, or dust should enter a nun’s eye, and she is unable to remove it or clean it out, then the monk who removes it or cleans it out does not transgress.
When a Nirgrantha takes hold of or supports a Nirgranthī who is stumbling or falling on a difficult path, on uneven ground, or on a mountain, he does not transgress [the rule].
When a Nirgrantha takes hold of or supports a Nirgranthī who is sinking or being swept away by mud, mire, moss, or water, he does not transgress [the rule].
When a Nirgrantha takes hold of or supports a Nirgranthī who is boarding or disembarking from a boat, he does not transgress [the rule].
A monk does not commit an offense by taking hold of or supporting a nun whose mind is distracted; he does not commit an offense by taking hold of or supporting a nun whose mind is deranged;
he does not commit an offense by taking hold of or supporting a nun who is possessed by a spirit.
A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who has fallen into a pit of illusion, does not transgress [the vow].
A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who has fallen into a pit of affliction, does not transgress [the vow].
A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who is involved in a cause for litigation, does not transgress [the vow].

A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who has committed an offense and is undergoing penance, does not transgress [the rule]. A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who has renounced food and drink, does not transgress [the rule].
A Nirgrantha, by taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī who is suffering from illness, does not transgress [the rule].

Six obstacles to the spiritual life (*kalpa*) are taught, namely: backbiting is an obstacle to self-restraint (*saṃyama*); frivolous speech is an obstacle to truthful speech; visual restlessness is an obstacle to the vigilance of movement (*īryāpathika*); greediness is an obstacle to the sphere of pure seeking (*eṣaṇā-gocara*); the greed for desires is an obstacle to the path of liberation (*mukti-mārga*); and making a basis for rebirth is an obstacle to the path of emancipation (*mokṣa-mārga*). In all respects, the Blessed One has praised freedom from worldly attachment (*anidānatā*). The duration of the spiritual life (*kalpasthiti*) is taught to be sixfold, namely: the duration of the spiritual life of one who observes the *sāmāyika* restraint.

The duration of the *chedovaṭṭhāvaṇiya* penance consists of: the duration while undergoing the penance (*sañjaya-kappaṭṭhitī*), the duration while ceasing from the penance (*nivvisamāṇa-kappaṭṭhitī*),
and the duration once the penance has been completed (*nivviṭṭhakāiya-kappaṭṭhitī*).
The duration of the Jinas' dispensation, the duration of the Elders' dispensation— thus I say.
